title: Values assigned to variables should match their type annotations
description: When variables are annotated with type hints in Python, the values assigned to them should match those type annotations. Type annotations serve as documentation and enable better static analysis, but assigning incompatible values defeats their purpose and can lead to runtime errors or unexpected behavior. While Python doesn't enforce type annotations at runtime, maintaining consistency between annotations and actual values improves code maintainability, readability, and helps catch potential bugs during development.
message: The value assigned to variable '{{variable_name}}' does not match its type annotation '{{expected_type}}'.

impact.reliability: Medium impact as type mismatches can lead to runtime errors and unexpected behavior in type-checked environments
impact.maintainability: High impact on code clarity as inconsistent type annotations make code harder to understand and maintain

recommendation: Either change the assigned value to match the type annotation, or update the type annotation to reflect the actual type being assigned. Consider using Union types if multiple types are legitimately expected.

references.title: SonarSource Python Rules - Values assigned to variables should match their type annotations
mypy - Static Type Checker for Python

noncompliant.code: age: int = "25"  # Type mismatch: string assigned to int annotation
name: str = 123  # Type mismatch: int assigned to str annotation
value: int = [1, 2, 3]  # Type mismatch: list assigned to int annotation
count: int = None  # Type mismatch: None assigned to non-optional int
numbers: List[int] = (1, 2, 3)  # Type mismatch: tuple assigned to List annotation

compliant.code: age: int = 25  # Correct: int assigned to int annotation
name: str = "John"  # Correct: str assigned to str annotation
numbers: List[int] = [1, 2, 3]  # Correct: List[int] assigned to List[int] annotation

from typing import Optional

count: Optional[int] = None  # Correct: None allowed in Optional[int]

from typing import Union

value: Union[int, str] = "hello"  # Correct: str is allowed in Union[int, str]

from typing import Dict

scores: Dict[str, int] = {"Alice": 95, "Bob": 87}  # Correct type match

why_is_this_an_issue: Type annotations in Python serve as both documentation and enable static type checking tools to catch potential errors. When values assigned to annotated variables don't match their declared types, it creates confusion for developers and defeats the purpose of type hints. This inconsistency can lead to runtime errors in type-checked environments, makes code harder to understand and maintain, and reduces the effectiveness of static analysis tools. Additionally, it can indicate logical errors or incomplete refactoring where the wrong type is being assigned to a variable.

how_to_fix.description: Identify the variable with the type annotation mismatch
Determine if the assigned value or the type annotation is correct
If the value is correct: Update the type annotation to match the actual type being assigned
If the annotation is correct: Change the assigned value to match the expected type
Consider using Union types if multiple types are legitimately expected
Use Optional[Type] for variables that can be None
Run static type checkers (mypy, pyright) to verify the fix

conditions.comment: Check if the assignment has a value (not just annotation)
Exclude None assignments to Optional types
